title: Patterns in Maths for Grade 1: Repeating, Growing & the Rule + Free Quiz
meta_title: Patterns in Maths for Grade 1 (+ Free Quiz)
meta_desc: See which patterns a Grade 1 child learns — repeating, growing, and finding the rule — with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: A bead necklace, a rangoli border, floor tiles — patterns are everywhere a six-year-old looks. Here is what your Grade 1 child actually learns about patterns, why it is early algebra in disguise, and a quick quiz to try.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Watch a Grade 1 child string a bead necklace — red, blue, red, blue — and you are watching maths happen. Not counting, not sums, but something that runs underneath both: the ability to spot a rule and say what comes next. Patterns in maths for Grade 1 are exactly this skill, and I would argue they matter more than most parents realise. A child who can look at red, blue, red, blue and confidently reach for red is doing, in miniature, the same thing an algebra student does when they finish a sequence.

The trouble is that patterns get treated as colouring-in filler — pretty, harmless, skippable. They are not. Below is what a six-year-old genuinely learns here, in the order it usually arrives, with the concrete Indian examples I lean on: rangoli borders, bead necklaces, and the tiles on a kitchen floor.

What counts as a pattern in Grade 1

A pattern is anything that follows a rule, so you can predict what comes next. In Grade 1 that splits neatly into two families: repeating patterns and growing patterns. Almost everything a child meets this year is one or the other, and telling them apart is half the lesson.

Repeating patterns and the ‘core’

A repeating pattern has a small chunk that repeats over and over. That chunk is the core (some NCERT-aligned books call it the unit). In red, blue, red, blue, the core is just red, blue. Find the core and the whole pattern opens up, because whatever came at the start of the core comes next after the end of it.

Children meet repeating patterns in three flavours, and it helps to name them out loud:

  • AB — two things alternating: clap, stamp, clap, stamp. Core is clap-stamp.
  • ABB — one, then two: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. Core is red-blue-blue.
  • ABC — three different things: circle, square, triangle, circle, square, triangle. Core is circle-square-triangle.

The letters are just a way of hearing the shape of the pattern without caring what the actual objects are. That is a surprisingly deep idea to hand a six-year-old — that a bead necklace and a clap-stamp rhythm can be the same pattern, AB, even though one is beads and one is sound. When a child sees that, they have grasped abstraction. That is early algebra, plainly.

Growing patterns

A growing pattern does not repeat — it changes by the same amount each step. A staircase of blocks where each step is one taller: 1, 2, 3, 4. Or counting in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8. The rule is not ‘what repeats’ but ‘what changes, and by how much’. Here the child has to notice the gap between the terms and keep applying it.

Growing patterns are harder, and I would not rush them. Get repeating patterns solid first — the core, the naming, the ‘what comes next’ — then bring in growing patterns as the plot twist: some patterns do not loop back, they climb.

Finding the rule — the whole point

Spotting what comes next is the visible skill. Finding the rule is the real one. Ask your child not just ‘what is next?’ but ‘how do you know?’ The answer you want is a rule stated out loud: ‘it goes red then blue, so after blue it must be red’ or ‘it jumps up by two each time.’ A child who can say the rule can extend the pattern forwards, backwards, and spot where it breaks.

That last one — spotting a broken pattern — is my favourite check. Show 2, 4, 6, 9, 10 and ask which number is wrong. A child who truly holds the rule ‘add two’ will pounce on the 9. A child who was only copying the look of the sequence will not. It separates real understanding from mimicry.

Patterns at a glance

Pattern typeExampleThe rule
AB repeatingred, blue, red, blue, …Core is red-blue; it just keeps looping
ABB repeatingclap, stamp, stamp, clap, stamp, stampCore is clap-stamp-stamp
ABC repeatingcircle, square, triangle, circle, …Core is circle-square-triangle
Growing (count in 2s)2, 4, 6, 8, …Add 2 each time
Growing (staircase)1, 2, 3, 4, …Each step is 1 taller

Why pattern-spotting is early algebra and number sense

Counting in twos, fives and tens — a Grade 1 staple — is nothing but a growing pattern, and it is the scaffolding for multiplication two years later. Number bonds hide a pattern too: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7 all make ten, and children who feel that rhythm learn their bonds faster. When we ask ‘what is the rule?’ we are quietly teaching the algebra question ‘what stays the same when the numbers change?’ without a single letter x in sight.

The number line itself is a pattern — each step is one more than the last. So a child comfortable with growing patterns is already at home with the idea that numbers march in a fixed, predictable order. That is number sense, and it pays off for years.

Making it real at home

You do not need worksheets to start. Patterns are already all over an Indian home. Point them out:

  • The border of a rangoli — ask your child to name the repeating core, then predict the next shape.
  • A bead or flower necklace — make one together and deliberately break the pattern once to see if they catch it.
  • Floor tiles or a bedsheet print — is it AB? ABB? Hunt for the core.
  • Clapping and stamping games — the best AB and ABB practice there is, and it needs nothing but hands.

One honest caveat: resist finishing the pattern for them. The five seconds of silence while a six-year-old works out that after blue comes red is the whole lesson. Jump in too soon and you have done the thinking they needed to do.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Patterns Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on repeating patterns, growing patterns and finding the rule. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A pattern goes red, blue, red, blue, red. What colour comes next?
questions.explanation: The core is red-blue and it keeps looping. After red always comes blue, so blue is next.

questions.q: In the pattern circle, square, circle, square, what is the repeating core?
questions.explanation: The smallest chunk that repeats is circle-square. That two-shape chunk is the core.

questions.q: Count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, __. What number comes next?
questions.explanation: This is a growing pattern with the rule add 2 each time. After 8 comes 8 + 2 = 10.

questions.q: A staircase grows 1, 2, 3, 4, __. How tall is the next step?
questions.explanation: Each step is 1 taller than the one before. After 4 the next step is 4 + 1 = 5.
The rule is add 5 each time: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. So 18 is the break — it should have been 20.

questions.q: The pattern is clap, stamp, stamp, clap, stamp, stamp. Which type of pattern is this?
questions.explanation: One clap then two stamps repeats. One thing then two of another is an ABB pattern.

questions.q: A bead necklace goes red, red, blue, red, red, blue. What are the next two beads?
questions.explanation: The core is red-red-blue. After the second blue the core starts again, so the next two beads are red, red.

questions.q: In the pattern triangle, star, moon, triangle, star, moon, what comes right after the second moon?
questions.explanation: The core is triangle-star-moon. After moon the core repeats from the start, so triangle comes next.

faq.q: What patterns does a Grade 1 child actually learn?
faq.a: Two main kinds: repeating patterns (AB, ABB and ABC with colours, shapes, sounds or objects) and growing patterns like counting in twos or a staircase getting one taller. In both cases the aim is to find the rule and say what comes next.

faq.q: What is the pattern core, and why does it matter?
faq.a: The core is the smallest chunk that repeats — in red, blue, red, blue it is just red-blue. Once a child finds the core, they can extend the pattern forever, because it simply loops. Finding the core is the key skill in repeating patterns.

faq.q: How are patterns connected to algebra?
faq.a: Patterns teach the question that algebra is built on: what is the rule, and what stays the same when the numbers change? Counting in twos is a growing pattern that becomes multiplication; spotting a rule is the same thinking as finishing a sequence — just without letters yet.

faq.q: My child can copy a pattern but cannot extend it. What helps?
faq.a: Copying is imitation; extending needs the rule. Ask ‘how do you know what comes next?’ and get them to say the rule out loud, like ‘red then blue, so after blue comes red’. Then try breaking a pattern on purpose and asking them to spot it — that forces real understanding.
